lessons.body:
Phase 02

The Monorepo Mental Model
Repository, workspace, package, application, dependency graph, and
why TaskFlow uses one repository without becoming one giant process.

Book 1 - Concepts

Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented

The Monorepo Mental Model
Before we create files, we need precise language. Most monorepo confusion comes from using repository,
workspace, project, application and package as if they mean the same thing. They do not.

One repository, multiple projects
A monorepo is one version-controlled repository that contains multiple related projects. pnpm calls the
package-management layer a workspace. Git knows about files and commits; pnpm knows which package.json files
belong to one dependency graph.

Repository vs               The .git directory makes taskflow a Git repository. pnpm-workspace.yaml makes
workspace                   the same folder a pnpm workspace root. One folder can be both, but the
responsibilities are different.

Repository and workspace are overlapping concepts

Git repository        same root        pnpm workspace            declares      Workspace packages

contains     contains

apps/web                     apps/api

Figure 1 - Git owns history; pnpm owns the multi-package dependency workspace

Four words you must separate
Term                         Meaning in this course

Repository                   The entire taskflow folder tracked by Git.

Workspace                    The pnpm-managed set of packages declared by pnpm-workspace.yaml.

Application                  A deployable product such as apps/web or apps/api.

Package                      A directory with its own package.json that participates in the workspace. An app is also a
package from pnpm's perspective.

Why one repository for TaskFlow?
The frontend and backend are separate applications, but they evolve together. A single repository lets one commit
represent a coherent system change: an API contract update, the matching frontend change, and any shared
validation change can be reviewed together.
•
One version-control history for related full-stack changes.
•
One workspace lockfile for consistent dependency resolution.
•
One place for repository-wide scripts and policy.
•
Easy local linking when a real shared package appears later.
•
A clear boundary between deployable apps and reusable packages.

Why not one giant application?
A monorepo does not mean one runtime process. Next.js and NestJS will remain independent applications with
different ports, build outputs, environment variables and deployment targets. They share a repository, not a process.

Repository unity does not erase runtime boundaries

taskflow repository

contains                         contains

apps/web - Next.js                                                      apps/api - NestJS

build/deploy                                                          build/deploy

frontend deployment                                                      API deployment

Figure 2 - One Git history can contain multiple independently deployable applications

The root is a control plane
The root package.json should coordinate the workspace, not become a dumping ground for application
dependencies. React belongs to the web package. NestJS belongs to the API package. A formatter or
repository-wide build orchestrator may eventually belong at the root because it acts across packages.

A useful ownership question
Which package imports this dependency at runtime or build time? If the answer is apps/web, install it there. If
the answer is apps/api, install it there. If the tool genuinely coordinates the entire repository, the root may own it.

apps/ versus packages/
Directory                 Responsibility                                  Examples later

apps/                     Deployable or runnable applications             web, api, worker

packages/                 Reusable code/config used by more than one      validators, shared types only when earned
workspace package

The dependency graph is the architecture you can compile
Once packages depend on one another, the workspace becomes a graph. Healthy graphs point toward reusable
foundations rather than creating cycles.

GOOD

apps/web      ----> packages/validators <----           apps/api

BAD

apps/web      ----> packages/shared ----> apps/api ----> apps/web

Cycle warning                     pnpm can detect cyclic workspace dependencies. A cycle usually means
responsibilities are mixed. Do not hide the warning; inspect which package
should stop depending on which other package.

Volume 01 - Engineering Foundation

One lockfile, strict declarations
pnpm workspaces use a shared lockfile by default. That gives the repository one exact dependency-resolution
snapshot while still keeping each package honest: a package should only access dependencies it declares in its own
package.json.

This matters because a monorepo should make dependency boundaries more visible, not less visible.

When a monorepo is the wrong tool
•
Projects have unrelated release cycles, ownership and security boundaries.
•
Teams cannot share repository access for compliance reasons.
•
The repository becomes a dumping ground for unrelated experiments.
•
Tooling complexity exceeds the coordination benefit.

TaskFlow is a good fit because the web and API are parts of one product and will share contracts, versions and
learning checkpoints.

Mental-model checkpoint
•
Git repository != pnpm workspace, even when they share the same root folder.
•
A workspace package has its own package.json.
•
An application is a package with a deployable runtime responsibility.
•
The root coordinates; it should not absorb every dependency.
•
Shared packages are introduced by reuse pressure, not by folder aesthetics.

lessons.title: Create the TaskFlow Root Repository
lessons.body:
Phase 02

Create the TaskFlow Root
Repository
A clean PowerShell build of the Git repository, pnpm workspace root,
version pins, lockfile, and structural directories.

Book 2 - Hands-on foundation

Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented

Create the TaskFlow Root Repository
Now we build the repository from nothing. The lesson is intentionally small: create the root, make it a Git repository,
establish package-manager metadata, and verify each file before frameworks enter the picture.

Step 1 - Choose the parent directory
Run repository-creation commands from the directory that should contain taskflow, not from inside another project.
This avoids accidental nested repositories and confusing workspace roots.

Get-Location
Get-ChildItem -Force

Example parent location:

C:\Users\<you>\Desktop\Projects

Step 2 - Create and enter the repository folder
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Name taskflow
Set-Location .\taskflow
Get-Location

Expected: the current path ends in taskflow. Do not continue until that is true.

Step 3 - Initialize Git
git init
git status

At this point Git knows the folder is a repository, but there are no committed files yet. The hidden .git directory
contains repository metadata; never edit it manually during normal work.

Step 4 - Create the minimal root package.json
Use the editor and create package.json at the repository root:

{
"name": "taskflow",
"version": "0.0.0",
"private": true,
"packageManager": "pnpm@12.4.2",
"engines": {
"node": ">=24.21.0 <25"
},
"scripts": {
"workspace:list": "pnpm list -r --depth -1"
}
}

Why private: true?          The root package exists to coordinate the repository. It is not a package we
intend to publish to a registry, so marking it private protects against accidental
publication.

Step 5 - Pin Node for the repository
Create a file named .node-version containing exactly:

24.21.0

fnm supports .node-version files. With automatic switching configured in Phase 01, entering the repository can select
the course Node version without relying on memory.

Step 6 - Create pnpm-workspace.yaml
packages:
- "apps/*"
- "packages/*"

pnpm requires pnpm-workspace.yaml at the workspace root. These patterns mean: any immediate child folder under
apps/ or packages/ that contains a package.json can participate as a workspace package.

Workspace globs describe where packages may live

pnpm-workspace.yaml

glob                               glob

apps/*                                                                 packages/*

future match                                                              future match

apps/web                                                           packages/validators

Figure 1 - The workspace file declares locations; it does not create packages by itself

Step 7 - Create the structural directories
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path .\apps -Force
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path .\packages -Force
Get-ChildItem -Force

Git and empty                     Git tracks files, not empty directories. If apps/ and packages/ are still empty at
directories                       commit time, they will not appear in a clone. That is fine. Phase 03 and later will
put real package files inside them. Do not create meaningless .gitkeep files just
to make the tree look complete.

Step 8 - Install the workspace
pnpm install

Because the workspace has no framework dependencies yet, the install should be small. Its important result is the
workspace lockfile: pnpm-lock.yaml. Commit that lockfile. It records exact dependency resolution for reproducible
installs.

Step 9 - Verify the root metadata
node --version
pnpm --version
pnpm run workspace:list
git status

At this point workspace:list may show only the root project because no app package exists yet. That is expected. A
workspace declaration is not the same as a populated workspace.

Expected repository on disk

|-- .git/
|-- .node-version
|-- apps/
|-- packages/

|-- pnpm-lock.yaml

Figure 2 - The repository is now both a Git repository and a pnpm workspace

A missing comma in package.json or incorrect indentation in YAML can make later framework generators appear
broken. When a tool fails before it starts meaningful work, inspect these root configuration files first.

correction                      layer that produced the failure: configuration syntax.

lessons.title: pnpm Workspaces and Dependency Boundaries
lessons.body:
Phase 02

pnpm Workspaces &
Dependency Boundaries
Workspace membership, the shared lockfile, strict dependencies, local
package linking, and where dependencies belong.

Book 3 - Workspace architecture

Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented

pnpm Workspaces and Dependency Boundaries
The root now exists. Before we add frameworks, we need to understand how pnpm decides what belongs to the
workspace and where dependencies should be installed.

The workspace file is a membership rule
pnpm-workspace.yaml sits at the root and defines package locations. The patterns apps/* and packages/* are
intentionally shallow: they match immediate package folders such as apps/web or packages/validators without
recursively pulling in arbitrary nested folders.

Workspace membership requires a package
A directory does not become a workspace package merely because it matches a glob. In practice it needs a
package.json. This distinction explains why an empty apps/ directory does not appear in pnpm recursive listings.

The shared lockfile
pnpm uses a single pnpm-lock.yaml at the workspace root by default. That makes dependency resolution reviewable
in one place and avoids one lockfile per application. The packages still declare their own dependencies; the lockfile
simply records the resolved graph for the workspace.

One workspace lockfile, separate dependency declarations

pnpm-lock.yaml

resolution           resolution          resolution

content-addressed files                   packages/validators
apps/web package.json                       apps/api   package.json
package.json

pnpm store

Figure 1 - The lockfile is shared; dependency ownership remains package-specific

Root dependency or package dependency?
Dependency type                       Where it belongs                                Example

Frontend runtime/build                apps/web                                        react, next
dependency

Backend runtime/build                 apps/api                                        @nestjs/core, fastify
dependency

Database dependency used by           apps/api initially                              prisma, @prisma/client, pg
API

Shared library dependency             the package that imports it                     zod inside validators, if that package
exists

Repository-wide developer tool        root only when genuinely                        possible formatter/orchestrator later
cross-workspace

The -w flag is an explicit root decision
pnpm protects workspace roots from accidental dependency installation. If you intentionally add a root dependency,
use the workspace-root flag so the decision is visible:

pnpm add -w -D <tool>

Do not respond to an ERR_PNPM_ADDING_TO_ROOT warning by blindly adding -w. First ask whether the
dependency actually belongs to the root.

Package-specific installs later
Once apps/web exists, a dependency can be targeted without changing directories:

pnpm --filter <package-name> add <dependency>

Filtering becomes powerful in larger workspaces, but directory-local installation is also fine when it is clearer. The
goal is correct ownership, not clever commands.

The workspace: protocol
When one workspace package genuinely depends on another, pnpm supports the workspace: protocol. It
guarantees the dependency resolves to a local workspace package instead of silently falling back to a registry
package.

{
"dependencies": {
"@taskflow/validators": "workspace:*"
}
}

Not yet                           We do not create @taskflow/validators in Phase 02. This is a mental model for
later. The package will be introduced only when both web and API have real
validation reuse.

Strict dependencies are a feature
pnpm is intentionally strict about package access. A package should not rely on a dependency simply because
another workspace package installed it. This prevents hidden dependencies that work on one machine and fail when
isolated.

Why we are not adding Turborepo yet
Task orchestration tools become useful when several packages have real dev, build, lint and test scripts. Right now
there are no applications to orchestrate. pnpm already gives us workspaces, recursive execution and filters, so
introducing another tool would add vocabulary without solving a present problem.

Future, not forbidden             Turborepo may become useful later for task graphs, caching and coordinated
builds. The teaching rule is not "never use Turbo"; it is "earn the abstraction
when the repository has enough work to orchestrate."

Version pins operate at different layers
File/field                            What it communicates

.node-version                         The exact Node version fnm should select for this repository.

engines.node                          The Node compatibility range expected by the package.

packageManager                        The pnpm version the repository expects.

Volume 01 - Engineering Foundation

File/field                       What it communicates

pnpm-lock.yaml                   The exact resolved dependency graph.

Dependency-boundary checkpoint
•
You can decide whether a dependency belongs to the root, web, API, or a future shared package.
•
You understand that one lockfile does not mean one package.json.
•
You know what workspace:* guarantees for local dependencies.
•
You will not create a shared package until at least two consumers need the same responsibility.
•
You know why root-install warnings should trigger reasoning rather than automatic flags.

lessons.title: Root Scripts and Workspace Commands
lessons.body:
Phase 02

Root Scripts & Workspace
Commands
Recursive execution, filters, command scope, and why the repository root
coordinates work without becoming another application.

Book 4 - Workspace operations

Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented

Root Scripts and Workspace Commands
The repository root is now a control plane. This book teaches the commands you will use to inspect and eventually
orchestrate packages, while keeping Phase 02 intentionally small.

Start with one script that has a job
Our root package.json contains only one repository-level script:

"scripts": {
"workspace:list": "pnpm list -r --depth -1"
}

That script answers a real question: which packages does pnpm currently see in the workspace? It is useful now and
remains useful later.

Recursive execution
The -r or --recursive flag runs a command across workspace packages. Once web and API exist, recursive
commands let the root coordinate common scripts without changing directories repeatedly.

pnpm -r --if-present run lint
pnpm -r --if-present run typecheck
pnpm -r --if-present run test

Why --if-present?
Different packages may not define every script at the same time while the course is evolving. --if-present lets a
repository-level command skip packages that do not define the requested script instead of failing immediately. Later,
when consistency matters, we may remove that leniency for specific checks.

Filtering
Filters target part of the workspace. After applications exist, you can run a command for a named package or
dependency graph instead of the entire repository.

pnpm --filter <package-name> run dev

Do not memorize complicated filter syntax yet. Learn the idea: recursion means many packages; filtering means a
selected subset.

Three ways to reach workspace scripts

root command

many              subset           alternative

-r / recursive                             --filter                        run inside package

runs                    runs              runs

web                                     api                                shared

Figure 1 - Choose the clearest command for the scope of work

Do not create future scripts before the packages exist
It is tempting to add dev, build, lint, test and typecheck scripts now because we know we will eventually need them.
Resist that urge. A root script should coordinate real package scripts. Phase 03 and 04 will create the applications,
then the root can acquire orchestration scripts that we can actually run and verify.

What the root package.json should look like now
{
"name": "taskflow",
"version": "0.0.0",
"private": true,
"packageManager": "pnpm@12.4.2",
"engines": {
"node": ">=24.21.0 <25"
},
"scripts": {
"workspace:list": "pnpm list -r --depth -1"
}
}

Future shape - not yet added
{
"scripts": {
"dev": "pnpm -r --parallel --if-present run dev",
"build": "pnpm -r --if-present run build",
"lint": "pnpm -r --if-present run lint",
"typecheck": "pnpm -r --if-present run typecheck",
"test": "pnpm -r --if-present run test"
}
}

This preview explains the destination. It is not an instruction to modify the Phase 02 root. We will add scripts only
when there are packages behind them.

Command scope is part of debugging
Question                                 Command

Where am I?                              Get-Location

What files exist, including dotfiles?    Get-ChildItem -Force

What packages does pnpm see?             pnpm run workspace:list

Which pnpm executable is running?        Get-Command pnpm

Which Node executable is running?        Get-Command node

What changed in Git?                     git status

Checkpoint
•
You understand root scripts as orchestration, not application logic.
•
You know the difference between recursive and filtered execution.
•
You can explain why the root currently has only workspace:list.
•
You can identify the working directory before running a command.
•
You know that adding more tooling is not progress unless it solves an observed problem.

Phase 02

Git Repository Hygiene
Ignore rules, line-ending normalization, README discipline, lockfile
policy, staged-diff review, and the first clean repository commit.

Book 5 - Repository hygiene

Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented

Git Repository Hygiene
A professional repository is defined as much by what it refuses to track as by what it commits. This book establishes
ignore rules, line-ending policy, documentation, the lockfile decision, and the first clean commit.

Create .gitignore
Use a repository-level .gitignore for files that every contributor should keep out of version control.

# Dependencies
node_modules/
.pnpm-store/

# Framework/build output
.next/
dist/
coverage/

# Logs
*.log

# Environment secrets
.env
.env.*
!.env.example

# OS noise
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db

Important Git rule
Adding a path to .gitignore does not untrack a file that was already committed. Ignore rules affect intentionally
untracked files. If a secret was committed, removing it from the working tree is not enough; treat it as exposed and
rotate the secret.

Create .gitattributes
Windows and Linux use different conventional line endings. Git can normalize text in the repository so diffs do not
become dominated by CRLF/LF noise.

* text=auto

*.sh text eol=lf
*.bat text eol=crlf
*.cmd text eol=crlf

*.png binary
*.jpg binary
*.jpeg binary
*.gif binary
*.pdf binary

Git documentation recommends text normalization and allows file-specific eol rules. We use a small policy: text is
normalized automatically, Unix shell scripts stay LF, Windows batch scripts check out as CRLF, and obvious binary
formats are marked binary.

Git hygiene acts at different points in the file lifecycle

Working tree                 git add        Staging area          git commit      Commit history

filters untracked                                                                     normalizes text

.gitignore                                                                           .gitattributes

Figure 1 - Ignore rules and attributes solve different problems

Create README.md
# TaskFlow

TaskFlow is the production-style project used by the

## Course baseline

- Node.js 24.21.0
- pnpm 12.4.2
- Windows-first development workflow

## Workspace

- apps/     deployable applications
- packages/ reusable packages introduced only when needed

## Current phase

Phase 02 - Monorepo, pnpm Workspaces and Repository Foundation

The README does not need to predict every future module. It records the repository purpose, baseline and current
structure. It will evolve as the product evolves.

Commit the lockfile
pnpm-lock.yaml belongs in version control for this application repository. package.json expresses dependency intent;
the lockfile records the exact resolved graph. Together they make installs reviewable and reproducible.

Inspect before staging
git status
git diff

Before git add, read the change set. This habit becomes more valuable as generated framework files appear in later
phases.

Stage intentionally and inspect again
git add .
git status
git diff --staged

Volume 01 - Engineering Foundation

The staged diff is the exact content about to become history. If node_modules, a secret, or a generated build folder
appears here, stop and correct the repository policy before committing.

First repository checkpoint commit
git commit -m "chore: initialize taskflow workspace"

The commit message describes the outcome rather than the commands used. A future reader should understand
why this point in history exists.

Expected committed files
.gitattributes
.gitignore
.node-version
README.md
package.json
pnpm-lock.yaml
pnpm-workspace.yaml

Where are apps/ and             They are empty, so Git may not show them. That is correct. Phase 03 and
packages/?                      Phase 04 will create real packages inside apps/.

There is no .env file in Phase 02, but our ignore policy is already ready for later phases. We allow .env.example
because it documents variable names without containing credentials. This is preventive engineering: establish the
safe default before secrets arrive.

•
node_modules and build outputs are ignored.

.env and .env.* are ignored, but .env.example can be committed.
•

Phase 02

Professional Monorepo
Workflow & Troubleshooting
A layer-by-layer diagnostic playbook for workspace roots, dependency
ownership, lockfiles, versions, line endings, Git state, and common setup
failures.

Book 6 - Debugging and workflow

Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented

Professional Monorepo Workflow and
Troubleshooting
Most setup failures are not mysterious. They are scope errors: wrong directory, wrong executable, wrong workspace
root, malformed configuration, or a file that Git is already tracking. This book gives you a repeatable diagnostic
sequence.

The six-question diagnostic loop
Question                             Evidence

1. Where am I?                       Get-Location

2. What files does this directory    Get-ChildItem -Force
contain?

3. Which executable is actually      Get-Command node / pnpm / git
running?

4. Which versions are active?        node --version / pnpm --version / git --version

5. Does pnpm see the expected        pnpm run workspace:list
workspace?

6. What does Git think changed?      git status / git diff / git diff --staged

Problem - command run from the wrong directory
Symptom: pnpm cannot find the expected workspace, package.json, or script. Diagnosis:

Get-Location
Get-ChildItem -Force

Correction: move to the directory containing the intended package.json or workspace root. Do not reinstall pnpm.

Problem - ERR_PNPM_ADDING_TO_ROOT
Symptom: pnpm warns that a dependency is being added to the workspace root. This warning is a decision
checkpoint, not a failure to suppress.
•
If the dependency belongs to apps/web, install it in or target apps/web.
•
If it belongs to apps/api, install it there.
•
If it truly coordinates the entire repository, use -w deliberately.
•
If you cannot explain the owner, do not install it yet.

Problem - multiple pnpm-lock.yaml files
Symptom: a lockfile appears inside an application in addition to the workspace root. That often means a package
was created or installed outside workspace awareness, or commands were run before the workspace root existed.

Diagnosis: inspect the repository tree and determine which lockfile belongs to the actual workspace. Avoid deleting
lockfiles blindly; understand how they were created first.

Problem - Node changed after reopening PowerShell
Check:

node --version
Get-Command node
Get-Content .\.node-version

If fnm automatic switching is configured, entering the repository should align Node with .node-version. If it does not,
debug the fnm shell initialization from Phase 01 rather than changing the repository version pin.

Problem - workspace package does not appear
Check whether the folder actually contains a package.json and whether its path matches the pnpm-workspace.yaml
glob. A folder name matching apps/* is not enough by itself.

Problem - endless line-ending changes
Symptom: Git shows files changed even though their text appears identical. Inspect .gitattributes and local Git
line-ending settings. Repository attributes should provide a predictable project-level policy. Avoid solving line-ending
noise by disabling normalization randomly per developer.

Problem - .env is still tracked after adding it to .gitignore
Git ignore rules do not stop tracking a file that is already in the index. If the file contained a real credential, rotate the
credential. Then remove it from version control history/index using an appropriate remediation workflow. Do not
assume adding .env to .gitignore makes an exposed secret safe.

Problem - nested .git directory
If git status inside a subfolder appears to show a completely different repository, someone may have run git init
inside the monorepo. Inspect hidden files with:

Get-ChildItem -Force -Recurse -Directory -Filter .git

A normal TaskFlow course repository should have one .git directory at the root. Remove a nested repository only
after confirming it is accidental and that no unique history is needed.

Debug the layer that produced the symptom

Observed symptom

where/version         json/yaml           git/lockfile

Check scope                                Check config                               Check state

evidence            evidence            evidence

Smallest correction

Figure 1 - Evidence narrows the problem before you change anything

A professional pre-commit rhythm
git status
git diff
# edit or verify
git add .
git diff --staged
# only then
git commit -m "..."

This rhythm is intentionally repetitive. It makes accidental secrets, generated output and unrelated changes visible
before they become history.

I can distinguish a pnpm warning from a Git problem or Node-version problem.
•
I prefer one small evidence-based correction over deleting node_modules or reinstalling everything.

Hands-On Lab, Exercises &
Phase Exit
Rebuild the workspace independently, diagnose realistic failures, reason
about dependency ownership, and prove readiness for Next.js.

Hands-On Lab, Exercises and Phase Exit
This book turns Phase 02 from reading into skill. The goal is not to remember a sequence of commands; it is to build
the repository from a clean parent folder and explain why every root file exists.

Lab - Rebuild the foundation without looking
Create a fresh practice folder outside your main course repository. From memory, reproduce the TaskFlow root
structure up to the first clean Git commit. Do not copy the reference files until after your attempt.

Lab requirements
•
Create a new folder and initialize Git.
•
Create package.json with name, version, private, packageManager, engines and workspace:list.
•
Create .node-version with the exact course Node version.
•
Create pnpm-workspace.yaml with apps/* and packages/*.
•
Run pnpm install and explain why pnpm-lock.yaml belongs in Git.
•
Create .gitignore and .gitattributes from memory, then compare with the reference.
•
Create a concise README.
•
Inspect git diff before staging and git diff --staged before committing.
•
Commit with a message that describes the checkpoint.

Level 1 - Follow
Run these verification commands in your practice repository and write down what each proves:

Get-Location
Get-ChildItem -Force
node --version
pnpm --version
pnpm run workspace:list
git status

Level 2 - Modify
Change the README to explain in your own words why apps/ and packages/ are different. Then use Git to inspect
the unstaged change, stage only README.md, inspect the staged diff, and unstage it without discarding your edit.

Hint: this exercise is about Git state, not about rewriting the entire repository.

Level 3 - Implement
Without changing directories into a future application, write the command you would use to add a dependency
specifically to a workspace package named @taskflow/web. Then explain why using -w instead would change
dependency ownership. Do not actually install a framework in Phase 02.

Level 4 - Engineer
A teammate proposes this repository immediately:

packages/
common/
types/
utils/
core/
shared/
config/
api-client/

Write a short design review. Which packages would you reject today, and what concrete reuse pressure would justify
creating one later? Your answer should reference responsibilities, not aesthetics.

Architecture tracing exercise
For each item below, identify its owner:

Item                                                      Possible owner

React                                                     root / apps/web / apps/api

@nestjs/core                                              root / apps/web / apps/api

Prisma CLI in the initial architecture                    root / apps/api / packages/db

A future shared Zod schema used by web and API            apps/web / apps/api / earned shared package

A repository-wide task orchestrator, if later adopted     root / apps/web / apps/api

Troubleshooting scenarios
Scenario A - Root warning
You are at taskflow/ and run pnpm add react. pnpm warns about adding a dependency to the workspace root. What
is the correct thought process?

Scenario B - Package missing
apps/web exists but pnpm workspace:list does not show it. What two conditions should you inspect first?

Scenario C - Secret tracked
You accidentally committed .env before adding the ignore rule. Why is editing .gitignore insufficient? What security
action may be necessary?

Scenario D - Empty folders vanish
After cloning your repository, apps/ and packages/ are missing. Is the clone broken? Explain Git's behavior and why
we intentionally avoided placeholder files.

Knowledge check
•
What makes taskflow a Git repository?
•
What makes taskflow a pnpm workspace?
•
Why is the root package.json marked private?
•
Why do we pin Node in both .node-version and engines.node?
•
Why should pnpm-lock.yaml be committed?
•
What does workspace:* guarantee?
•
Why is ERR_PNPM_ADDING_TO_ROOT useful?
•
What is the difference between .gitignore and .gitattributes?
•
Why are Next.js and NestJS not installed at the root?
•
Why did we avoid Turborepo and shared packages in this phase?

Answer guide
Repository: the .git directory created by git init. Workspace: the root pnpm-workspace.yaml plus matching
packages. private: prevents accidental publication of the coordination package. Version pins: .node-version drives
fnm selection while engines communicates compatibility. Lockfile: reproducible resolved dependency graph.
workspace:* requires local workspace resolution. Root warning: forces explicit dependency ownership. .gitignore:

Volume 01 - Engineering Foundation

controls intentionally untracked files; .gitattributes: controls file attributes such as text normalization. Framework
ownership: install where imported. No Turbo/shared packages yet: no current problem requires them.

•
I can recreate the repository without copy/pasting every command.
•
I can explain every root file in one sentence.
•
I can identify whether a dependency belongs to the root, web, API or a future shared package.
•
I understand that the monorepo is one repository with multiple independent application runtimes.
•
I can inspect Git state before and after staging.
•
I can diagnose workspace-root and version-scope problems systematically.
•
My main TaskFlow repository has a clean checkpoint commit.

Next - Phase 03: Next.js Fundamentals
We finally have a trustworthy home for the frontend. In Phase 03 we will create apps/web as the first real workspace
package and teach Next.js as an application runtime rather than as a generator command. The architecture will
evolve from a repository with no application runtime to Browser -> Next.js.

serves UI to

Browser

Phase 02

Workspace Command
Reference & Practical Patterns
A compact, intent-driven reference for PowerShell orientation, pnpm
workspace scope, dependency installation, recursive scripts, and Git
inspection.

Book 8 - Command reference

Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented

Workspace Command Reference and Practical
Patterns
This reference book keeps the commands you will use most often in one place, but each command is grouped by
intent rather than presented as a memorization list. The point is to choose the right scope deliberately.

Repository orientation commands
Intent                       PowerShell command                  What it proves

Current directory            Get-Location                        Which folder receives relative paths and local config
lookup

Visible and hidden items     Get-ChildItem -Force                Whether .git, dotfiles and root files actually exist

Resolve Node executable      Get-Command node                    Which node.exe PowerShell will launch

Resolve pnpm executable      Get-Command pnpm                    Which pnpm command PowerShell will launch

Git repository state         git status                          Tracked/untracked/staged state in the current
repository

Workspace inspection commands
pnpm run workspace:list
pnpm list -r --depth -1
pnpm root -w

workspace:list is our repository script. pnpm list -r --depth -1 is the underlying recursive package view. pnpm root
-w is useful later when diagnosing where the workspace-level node_modules is located.

Dependency installation patterns
Situation                          Pattern                                   Reasoning

Install in current package         pnpm add                                  Use when your shell is already inside
the owning package

Install in named package           pnpm --filter add                         Useful from the root when ownership is
already clear

Install root dev tool              pnpm add -w -D                            Explicitly states that the workspace root
owns the tool

Local workspace dependency         workspace:* in package.json               Guarantees local workspace resolution
instead of registry fallback

Recursive script patterns - for later phases
pnpm -r --if-present run lint
pnpm -r --if-present run typecheck
pnpm -r --if-present run test
pnpm -r --parallel --if-present run dev

These become useful after packages define the corresponding scripts. --parallel makes sense for long-running
development servers that should run together; build-like tasks often benefit from dependency-aware ordering
instead.

Git inspection patterns

git status
git diff
git add <path>
git diff --staged
git restore --staged <path>
git commit -m "message"

The sequence matters more than the individual commands. Inspect -> stage intentionally -> inspect the staged
snapshot -> commit. This is the workflow that protects the repository from accidental noise and secrets.

The command-selection loop

Orient       where/which package   Decide scope        root/filter/local   Run command

next decision      status/output

Verify result

Figure 1 - A professional workflow starts with scope, not with the command itself

Commands we intentionally postpone
•
Framework generators - introduced only when the relevant app phase begins.
•
Turbo task graph commands - postponed until there are several real scripts worth orchestrating.
•
Prisma commands - database architecture begins in Volume 03, with Prisma 7.9.1 locked.
•
Docker and deployment commands - postponed until the application works locally and is testable.

Quick reference checklist
Before any workspace command, answer three questions: Where am I? Which package owns this change? How
will I verify the result? If you cannot answer those questions, the command is premature.

Phase 02

Repository Design Decisions &
Anti-Patterns
Why the TaskFlow root stays boring, which abstractions we rejected, and
the evidence that would justify adding them later.

Book 9 - Architecture decisions

Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented

Repository Design Decisions and Anti-Patterns
The strongest repository architecture is usually the one with the fewest unexplained moving parts. This book records
the decisions Phase 02 made, the alternatives we rejected, and the signals that would justify changing those
decisions later.

Decision 1 - One monorepo for web and API
Choice                      Why now                                     Revisit when...

One Git repository          The applications form one product and       access, compliance, ownership or
change together                             release boundaries become truly
independent

pnpm workspace              Built-in multi-package management already   a future orchestrator must solve
solves our current problem                  measurable task-graph/caching pain

One shared lockfile         Consistent resolution and easier review     almost never for this single-product
workspace without a concrete reason

Decision 2 - Keep the root boring
The root is policy and orchestration. A root package that accumulates React, NestJS, database libraries and
application utilities has erased the very ownership boundaries the monorepo was meant to clarify.

Smell                     If you cannot tell whether a dependency is frontend, backend, or repository
tooling because everything is installed at the root, the package boundaries are
already failing.

Decision 3 - Do not create packages before reuse exists
A folder named shared is not architecture. A shared package earns its existence when it owns one coherent
responsibility that at least two consumers need and when keeping duplicate implementations would create real drift
or risk.

Good future package candidate
A validators package can become reasonable after web and API both need the same task input schema and we
intentionally want one authoritative contract.

Weak package candidate
A utils package that collects unrelated date helpers, string functions, API wrappers and business rules becomes a
dependency magnet. Prefer colocating helpers with the feature or responsibility they support until a coherent
reusable package emerges.

Anti-pattern - the prebuilt enterprise tree
packages/
common/
core/
domain/
infrastructure/
shared/
utils/
types/
config/

The problem is not the names themselves. The problem is creating them before the system contains responsibilities
that require those boundaries. Empty architecture makes navigation harder while teaching nothing about why the
abstraction exists.

Anti-pattern - framework dependencies at root
taskflow/package.json
react
next
@nestjs/core
prisma
@prisma/client

This makes the root look convenient while hiding which app truly depends on each technology. The correct default is
package ownership: frontend libraries in apps/web, backend/database libraries in apps/api initially.

Anti-pattern - multiple nested repositories
Running git init inside apps/web or apps/api creates independent histories unless intentionally using submodules or
another advanced strategy. That would undermine the course monorepo model. One .git directory at taskflow/ is the
expected state.

Anti-pattern - generated files without review
Framework generators are useful, but generated output is still your codebase. Starting in Phase 03, every generator
step must be followed by tree inspection and Git diff review before the generated code is accepted.

How architecture should evolve

Observed need          problem first   Smallest option         implement/test         Verify benefit

no clear gain           repeated pressure

Keep simple                                    Earn abstraction

Figure 1 - Abstractions are responses to evidence, not decorations chosen in advance

Decision record for future phases
•
Phase 03 creates apps/web and lets Next.js own frontend dependencies.
•
Phase 04 creates apps/api and lets NestJS/Fastify own backend dependencies.
•
Prisma remains inside apps/api when introduced; no packages/db is created by default.
•
A shared validators package is considered only when real cross-app schema reuse appears.
•
Turborepo is considered only when pnpm orchestration becomes measurably insufficient.
•
Deployment remains independent per app even though source history is shared.

Engineering checkpoint
A clean Phase 02 repository is intentionally unimpressive to look at. That is a strength. Every file at the root has a
concrete responsibility, and there is almost nothing to delete. The sophistication will come from working software and
earned boundaries, not from an elaborate empty tree.

Debugging Workshop — Phase 02: Monorepo, pnpm Workspaces & Repository Foundation

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
Repository root -> pnpm-workspace.yaml -> apps/* -> packages/* -> workspace dependencies -> root scripts -> Turbo/task graph

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Installing app-only dependencies at workspace root
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Duplicating tsconfig settings in every package
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — Using relative imports across app boundaries instead of package contracts
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 4 — Committing build output, environment files, or node_modules
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Monorepo, pnpm Workspaces & Repository Foundation

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 02 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Create a pnpm monorepo whose boundaries, scripts, shared configuration, and dependency ownership are understandable before feature code grows.

Required artifact
TaskFlow repository root with apps/web, apps/api, shared packages, workspace metadata, root scripts, and clean Git hygiene.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can explain workspace protocol dependencies.
• Can run one app and the whole repository intentionally.
• Can identify dependency ownership.
• Can add a shared package without circular dependencies.

Independent build sequence
1. Create the repository root and initialize Git before generating applications.
2. Declare workspace globs and explain why apps and packages are separate categories.
3. Create web and API workspaces without copying node_modules between them.
4. Create a shared TypeScript configuration package and consume it through workspace dependencies.
5. Add root dev/build/typecheck/test scripts that delegate to workspaces.
6. Inspect pnpm why/list output so you can explain where a dependency is owned and why.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.
